hook: The scholar turned mystic poet whose verses of love are read around the world.

pages.x: Jalal al-Din Rumi was born in 1207 in Balkh, in what is now Afghanistan. As the Mongols drew near, his father, a preacher, led the family west on a journey of thousands of kilometres. They settled in Konya, in Anatolia, then called Rum, which gave Rumi his name.
After his father died, Rumi became a famous teacher of Islamic law in Konya, with hundreds of students. He was a serious, sober scholar, and wrote no poetry at all.

In 1244 he met a wild wandering dervish, Shams of Tabriz. A legend says Shams threw Rumi's books into a fountain, then pulled them out dry. The two became inseparable. Jealous students drove Shams away, and when he vanished for good, perhaps murdered, Rumi, heartbroken, began to write poetry.

He poured out tens of thousands of verses. His Masnavi, some 25,000 couplets of stories and teachings, opens with a reed flute crying for the reed bed it was cut from, like the soul longing for God. Persians call it "the Quran in Persian".

Rumi would turn and turn as he recited poetry. After his death his son founded the Mevlevi order, whose dervishes whirl to music in long white robes, one hand raised to heaven and one turned to the earth. They still whirl in Konya today.
He died in Konya in 1273. Christians, Jews and Muslims all walked in his funeral procession. His followers call his death his "wedding night", his union with God, and celebrate it every December.
Rumi is one of the greatest poets of the Persian language, and has become one of the best-selling poets in the United States. His poems of love, longing and joy speak across faiths and centuries.
pts: Wrote the Masnavi, a masterpiece of Persian poetry
One of the most widely read poets in the world today
